title: Chicks rank 20 greatest songs to mark 20th anniversary of Taking the Long Way
content:
The country trio, once known as the Dixie Chicks, are celebrating the 20th anniversary of their album *Taking the Long Way* with a countdown of their 20 greatest songs. This list highlights the band’s catchy and sometimes controversial catalogue, noting that their consistency is as remarkable as the sheer number of hits they have produced.

One entry on the list is "If I Fall…," which was one of eight singles released from the album *Fly*. The song is described as organ-driven rock that features a Nashville twang from the fiddle, characterized by a confident energy that suggests the band knows they cannot put a foot wrong.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey Leads 2025 Oscars Race Amidst Festival Underwhelm
content:
The 2025 fall film festival season, spanning Venice, Telluride, and Toronto, was described as notably underwhelming and marked by a general lack of buzz. This period occurred months after *Sinners* transitioned from a box-office hit to an awards contender and simultaneously with *One Battle After Another*, which bypassed festivals to win best picture. The article notes that the traditional pipeline for producing Oscar winners, which previously yielded films like *Birdman*, *Spotlight*, *12 Years a Slave*, and *The King’s Speech*, has diminished in influence, with *Nomadland* cited as the last fall festival film to win the top prize.

Industry trades attribute part of the season’s lackluster performance to studios avoiding the risk of bad buzz and potential embarrassment for A-listers, contrasting successful films like *The Shape of Water* and *Poor Things* with lower-received titles such as *White Noise* and *Joker: Folie à Deux*. Consequently, while the upcoming season features new films starring Tom Cruise, Timothée Chalamet, Anne Hathaway, Christian Bale, Amy Adams, Daisy Edgar-Jones, Ben Affleck, and Mikey Madison, none of these productions are scheduled to brave a festival premiere. Christopher Nolan’s *The Odyssey* is identified as a potential frontrunner, though a group of competitors is beginning to emerge.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Disney, Apple, and Peacock raise streaming service prices
content:
US consumers are increasingly opting out of the streaming world as multiple services raise prices without providing significant additional benefits. Disney recently increased the cost of most Disney+ and Hulu service iterations and bundles by a couple of dollars per month, with only specific ad-supported bundles remaining at their previous price points. The company’s terms of service state that it reserves the right to insert ads before and after programming on any subscription tier, regardless of the payment level.

Price increases have become a common trend across the industry, prompting The Verge to maintain a dedicated page for such news. Apple has raised its prices four times in four years, while Peacock subscribers have seen their monthly bills increase by five or six dollars since the summer of 2025, including a recent hike last month. Netflix, which has not raised prices since March 2026, is noted to likely be approaching another price increase.
author: Guardian Culture

title: Chef‑turned author Louise Kennedy addresses second book syndrome
content:
Louise Kennedy, a chef who has become an award‑winning author, remains unfazed by the pressure often associated with writing a second book. She has publicly addressed the so‑called “second book syndrome,” maintaining confidence in her creative process.

In a recent statement, Kennedy urged readers to “give anything they fancy a lash,” encouraging experimentation and boldness in pursuing new projects. This advice underscores her belief that creative exploration should be embraced without hesitation.
author: BBC Entertainment

title: US Jockey Club orders renaming of racehorse Austrian Painter
content:
The US Jockey Club has ordered that the racehorse Austrian Painter be renamed after an investigation found the name was a reference to Adolf Hitler. The horse, which won its debut race at the Horseshoe Indianapolis track on Monday, also has a full sister named New Order. A complaint about the name prompted the club to begin a review.

Hitler, born in Austria, was a professional artist in Vienna before the First World War. The term “Austrian Painter” is sometimes used online to discuss Hitler without naming him, a practice that helps users avoid content‑moderation filters. The investigation concluded that the horse’s name was linked to that reference, leading to the renaming order.

The US Jockey Club has ordered the name change, citing the reference to Adolf Hitler as the reason for the action.
author: Guardian Sport

title: My bad TV history qualifies me to discuss Disney’s women’s football coverage | Max Rushden
content:
Max Rushden argues that his extensive history of producing low-quality television and radio programs qualifies him to critique Disney’s coverage of women’s football. He notes that while a golden retriever and a pasta-guessing segment were unusual features in a Women’s Champions League show, he understands how such elements arrived in the broadcast. Rushden acknowledges that he has created many bad TV programs, below-average radio shows, and numerous podcasts that will not be remembered, though he has also produced some good and great programs, including unreferenced segments in the Soccer AM studio.

Rushden states that he has hosted shows with varying levels of editorial control, ranging from near-complete autonomy to roles where he could have been replaced by a performing monkey. He concludes by noting that he has had more awful ideas than great ones, using this personal track record to frame his perspective on the specific programming choices made in the women’s football coverage.
author: Guardian Sport

title: Northampton lead Prem charge but history shows title defence will be no simple task | Robert Kitson
content:
Northampton have retained Henry Pollock and are eager to improve as they prepare to defend their English domestic title, though the path to success is expected to be challenging due to the resurgence of rivals such as Saracens and Exeter. The Saints, who are aiming for a third title in four years, won the championship in June, a feat that has become increasingly rare in the league's history.

The difficulty of retaining the trophy is highlighted by the fact that no club has successfully defended the English domestic title in a long time, with the last team to achieve consecutive wins being Saracens in 2019. Phil Dowson, the Northampton leader, emphasizes that while his team performed exceptionally well last season, that period is now in the past. The current landscape makes "doubling up" a nearly obsolete concept, as the league has moved away from the era of serial winners like Bath, Leicester, and Saracens.
author: Guardian Sport

title: England v Sri Lanka: Second ODI Live Coverage
content:
The second men’s one-day international between England and Sri Lanka is underway at Headingley, with live over-by-over updates commencing at 12.30pm BST. The venue is noted as typically favorable for batting, leading to expectations that Sri Lanka may target a score of upwards of 300. In the opening over, Sri Lanka scored one run with Nissanka on one and Kamindu Mendis on zero, as Archer delivered an accurate spell that saw Mendis play out five consecutive dot balls.

The live coverage includes additional updates on the County Championship finale and the match between South Africa and Australia. The initial report highlights the long duration of the fifty-over format, suggesting it allows players like Kamindu Mendis time to settle in. The current status of the match reflects the start of the innings with the specified score and player statistics from the first over.
author: Guardian Sport

title: 11-Year-Old Yuki Kurihara Becomes Youngest Asian Games Athlete
content:
Yuki Kurihara, an 11-year-old primary school student, is making history as the youngest athlete participating in this year's Asian Games. The young competitor has made a flying start in his athletic career, distinguishing himself among the other participants at the event.

Kurihara’s presence at the Asian Games marks a significant milestone for the young student, who is currently in primary school. His participation highlights his early achievement in the competitive sports arena.
author: BBC Sport

title: Premier League 'Bermuda Triangle' Meme Stats
content:
Social media has popularized a meme suggesting that Bournemouth, Brighton, and Brentford constitute a Premier League "Bermuda Triangle" where visiting teams consistently lose points. The premise of this narrative is currently being examined to determine if statistical data supports the claim that these three clubs are particularly difficult opponents for their rivals.

The central question surrounding this topic is whether the available statistics validate the social media trend or if it remains an unsupported anecdote. The analysis focuses specifically on the performance records of teams playing against these three clubs to assess the validity of the "Bermuda Triangle" label.
author: BBC Sport

title: George Russell Tops Both Baku Practice Sessions
content:
Mercedes driver George Russell recorded the fastest times in both Friday practice sessions for the Azerbaijan Grand Prix in Baku. He outpaced his rival, Antonelli, to lead the timing sheets for the day's initial track activities.

Russell's performance established him as the quickest driver on the circuit during the opening sessions of the weekend.
author: BBC Sport

title: Man City Uses 650,000-Entry Database for Squad Rebuild
content:
BBC Sport has provided an inside look at Manchester City’s data team, highlighting their significant role in the club’s squad overhaul over the past 18 months. The report details how the team utilized a database containing 650,000 entries to guide the rebuild of the squad.

This data-driven approach has been a key component of Manchester City’s recent strategic efforts to restructure their player roster.
author: BBC Sport

title: Fury and Joshua to Fight in Cardiff on December 11
content: Cardiff’s Principality Stadium is set to host the all-British heavyweight boxing match between Anthony Joshua and Tyson Fury on 11 December. The event has been officially announced for the specified date and venue. This scheduled bout brings the two fighters together in a contest within the United Kingdom.
author: BBC Sport

title: Andy Burnham Supports Repealing Football Alcohol Ban
content: Andy Burnham has consistently advocated for the repeal of the ban that prohibits football supporters from consuming alcohol in the view of the pitch. Despite his long-standing support for this change, the question remains whether fans themselves actually desire the removal of this restriction.
author: BBC Sport

title: Trump's FDA Nominee Heidi Overton Faces Senate Confirmation Hearing
content:
Dr. Heidi Overton, President Trump’s nominee to head the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), is set to appear before the Senate Committee on Health, Education, Labor and Pensions (HELP) on Thursday for her confirmation hearing. As a White House domestic policy aide and preventive medicine physician, Overton is seeking approval to lead the agency.

During the proceedings, Overton is anticipated to address inquiries regarding vaccines. The hearing represents a key step in the process for her to assume leadership of the FDA.
author: The Hill

title: Sen. John Kennedy Labels Iranian Leaders Part of Reptile Colony
content:
Sen. John Kennedy (R-La.) stated on Wednesday that Iranian leaders are “part of a colony of reptiles,” a description that groups them with other U.S. adversaries including China, Russia, and North Korea. The senator made these comments while appearing on Fox News’ Will Cain show.

Kennedy provided this assessment in response to a question regarding President Trump’s attendance at the United Nations General Assembly in New York City. The exchange highlighted the senator’s characterization of these foreign governments during the discussion.
author: The Hill

title: Obama claims federal government is less corrupt than ever
content:
Former President Obama stated in his newly launched literary-focused podcast that the federal government is currently “so much less corrupt” than it has been in the past. He noted that people are often surprised by this assessment, explaining that the reduction in corruption pertains specifically to pure bribes, patronage, or favors.

The former president emphasized that the current level of government integrity is significantly higher than historical standards regarding these specific types of misconduct.
author: The Hill

title: US Border Security Recommendations Remain Unimplemented
content:
The 9/11 Commission has already identified specific weaknesses in border security, meaning the government does not require a new body to conduct further investigations. The existing recommendations provide a clear framework for addressing these vulnerabilities, rendering additional commissions unnecessary for the task of identification.

The primary focus remains on completing the work already outlined by the Commission rather than initiating new inquiries. The path forward involves executing the established security measures to resolve the identified gaps in the system.
author: The Hill

title: Trump: Wants to leave AI status quo ahead of Xi talks
content:
President Trump stated on Thursday that he intends to leave artificial intelligence “exactly where it is” in anticipation of discussions with Chinese President Xi Jinping. In a post on Truth Social, Trump described the upcoming meeting as a “big day” and identified Super Intelligence (SI) as a major subject of the conversation.

The President’s comments highlight his specific stance on the technological topic ahead of the bilateral talks. He reiterated his desire to maintain the current status of AI while addressing the broader implications of Super Intelligence with his Chinese counterpart.
author: The Hill

title: The Senate map expands: Which states are now in play
content:
The competition for control of Congress is intensifying as an increasing number of Senate races become viable opportunities for both political parties. This expansion of the electoral map raises questions about which states are becoming accessible to new challengers and which incumbents may face greater vulnerability in the upcoming cycle.

In addition to the shifting dynamics of individual Senate races, there are emerging warning signs for Republicans among independent voters. The analysis also considers the potential for 2026 to set a modern record for congressional turnover, highlighting the broader implications of these trends for the balance of power in the legislature.
author: The Hill

title: Rep. Madeleine Dean says she worries more about Republicans complicit with Trump than democratic socialists
content:
Democratic Representative Madeleine Dean of Pennsylvania told reporters on Wednesday that she is “far less worried” about the prospect of democratic socialists entering the House than she is about Republican lawmakers she described as “complicit” with President Trump. Dean’s comments focused on her relative concern for a candidate who “espouses some DSA [Democratic Socialists of America] title winning and coming into our caucus” compared with Republicans she views as aligned with Trump.

The representative’s remarks underscore her assessment that the presence of Republicans she deems complicit with the former president poses a greater issue for the chamber than the potential election of a democratic socialist. Dean’s statement reflects her prioritization of perceived partisan alignment over ideological labels within the House.
author: The Hill

title: Warren Criticizes Trump's Greeting of Xi Jinping
content: Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.) criticized President Trump on Wednesday for his unusual decision to greet Chinese President Xi Jinping with fanfare during the leader's arrival at Joint Base Andrews. Speaking to CNN’s Kaitlan Collins, the senator stated that the behavior is consistent with Trump’s character, asserting that he loves dictators and the power that Xi Jinping represents.
author: The Hill

title: Xi Jinping Arrives in U.S. for First State Visit in 11 Years
content: Chinese leader Xi Jinping arrived in the United States on Wednesday evening. This visit marks his first state visit to the country in 11 years. The leader's arrival initiates the official diplomatic engagement.
author: NPR Politics

title: Trump-Xi Summit Analysis by Former Biden Administration Official
content:
NPR’s A Martinez posed a question about the upcoming Trump‑Xi summit.  
The question, “What can we expect from the Trump‑Xi summit?” was directed to Daniel Kritenbrink, who serves as the assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific affairs in the Biden administration.  

Kritenbrink’s role as assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific affairs places him in a position to comment on the diplomatic implications of the meeting between former President Trump and Chinese President Xi.  

NPR’s A Martinez asked Daniel Kritenbrink, assistant Secretary of State for East Asian and Pacific affairs, about expectations for the Trump‑Xi summit.
author: NPR Politics

title: Newcastle University Faces Backlash Over Anant Ambani's Sustainability Professorship
content:
Newcastle University is facing backlash from conservationists over the appointment of Anant Ambani, the son of India’s richest person, as a professor of sustainability. The university announced that Ambani, who also runs a controversial mega-zoo, had been granted a professorship of practice in recognition of his work in conservation, biodiversity protection, animal welfare, and environmental stewardship, as well as his significant contributions to advancing a more sustainable future.

The decision has met with incredulity and criticism from environmental groups. The controversy centers on the contrast between the academic title of professor of sustainability and Ambani’s background as an heir to an Indian oil and gas fortune.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Fossil-fuel firms in line for billions in benefits after answering Trump’s donation call
content:
A new report released by Senator Sheldon Whitehouse, ranking member of the Senate environment and public works committee, and Senate Democratic leader Chuck Schumer, states that the fossil fuel industry secured an estimated $190 billion in tax breaks and subsidies over the next decade. According to the senators, this outcome followed the industry’s response to Donald Trump’s pre-election call for major campaign donations, resulting in higher bills for American taxpayers and public health costs associated with pollution.

The report, published on Thursday, details what the senators describe as the fossil fuel industry’s expansive influence over the Trump administration, characterizing the arrangement as a bargain between the president and major polluters.
author: Guardian Environment

title: Climate change expands extreme heat threat to human health
content: A personal account from rural New South Wales, Australia, describes a severe heat wave experienced by the author at age 12 during the summer vacation following Christmas. The narrative details the conditions inside a tin-roofed house, where sheets were draped over the front windows to act as curtains while the author spent long, hot hours working on a 1,000-piece puzzle at the kitchen table. This individual experience is presented within the context of climate change expanding the threat of extreme heat to human health.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study Links Chronic Stress to Cognitive Decline Differences
content:
A new study led by researchers at the Wake Forest University School of Medicine suggests that chronic stress and perceived social support may influence how memory and thinking abilities change with age. The research indicates that these factors are linked to differences in cognitive decline across specific demographic groups.

The findings highlight the potential impact of stress and social support on aging cognitive functions, offering insights into the variations observed among different populations.
author: Medical Xpress

title: AI tool finds biological signals in the gut microbiome that other methods miss, may flag early signs of disease
content:
University of Missouri researchers have developed a new machine-learning tool designed to identify biological signals within the human gut microbiome that are typically overlooked by conventional methods. The Mizzou team, which combines expertise in medicine, data science, and engineering, utilized artificial intelligence to uncover hidden clues among the trillions of bacteria residing in the gut. These findings include changes that could potentially assist scientists in detecting diseases at an earlier stage.

The research team’s work, which focuses on analyzing the complex ecosystem of gut bacteria, has been published in the journal mSystems. This new approach aims to reveal subtle biological indicators that other methods fail to capture, providing a novel pathway for understanding the role of the microbiome in health and disease.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Griffith University research links breath tests to lung cancer detection
content:
New research from Griffith University suggests that analyzing human breath could help identify cancerous lung nodules, potentially reducing the reliance on invasive testing. The study focused on examining exhaled breath to assist medical professionals in differentiating between cancerous and noncancerous nodules, a process that supports earlier diagnosis of lung cancer.

Given that approximately 2.5 million new cases of lung cancer are diagnosed annually, this breath-based approach offers a potential tool for improved detection. The findings indicate that exhaled breath analysis may serve as a method to distinguish between benign and malignant lung nodules.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Sudden Infant Deaths Rise Among Black Babies, Widening Mortality Gap
content:
New research published in the journal JAMA Network Open indicates that rates of sudden unexpected infant deaths (SUID) have begun to rise after years of declines. The study highlights that this increase is particularly pronounced among babies born to Black mothers.

These findings help explain a puzzling widening of the disparity in infant mortality rates between white and Black populations since 2020. The research provides context for the recent shift in mortality trends affecting these specific demographic groups.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Study examines mindfulness and self-stigma in university students
content:
The question of whether mindfulness is linked to improved mental health and reduced self-stigma among university students is framed by the common experience of exclusion faced by many minority groups. Individuals who are denied full social acceptance due to being perceived as having a "lesser" status or value may internalize this stigma, leading to feelings of being different, lesser, or unwanted.

This internalization of stigma serves as a key context for examining the potential benefits of mindfulness practices in academic settings.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Data expertise aids researchers in analyzing clinical tool usage
content:
Clinical decision-support tools are designed to assist clinicians in making evidence-based decisions, accessing relevant patient information, and navigating complex care. Despite these capabilities, the mere availability of such tools within an electronic health record (EHR) does not ensure that clinicians will incorporate them into their routine practice.

Data expertise enables researchers to better understand how these clinical tools are utilized in real-world settings. This analytical approach helps bridge the gap between tool availability and actual adoption by healthcare providers.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Starbucks to Close 250 North American Stores
content:
Starbucks has announced it will close approximately 250 stores, representing about 1% of its North American cafes, as part of the latest stage in its corporate turnaround. This decision marks the most recent round of cafe closures for the company.

The move aligns with Starbucks' ongoing efforts to restructure its operations within North America.
author: CNBC Business

title: Lowe's is launching a drone delivery service in partnership with DoorDash, Alphabet
content:
Lowe's is set to launch a drone delivery service in a partnership with DoorDash and Alphabet's Wing, according to exclusive information obtained by CNBC. The initiative marks a collaborative effort between the home improvement retailer and the two technology firms to integrate aerial logistics into its operations.

This new service represents a strategic move for Lowe's to expand its delivery capabilities through the combined expertise of its partners. The announcement highlights the growing trend of major retailers adopting drone technology to enhance customer convenience and operational efficiency.
author: CNBC Business

title: JoAnn Fabrics Fans Form Crafts Co-op to Replace Bankrupt Retailer
content:
US crafters are organizing to establish a communal network aimed at filling the void left by JoAnn Fabrics, a store that served as a vital hub for small businesses including wedding dress makers, upholsters, milliners, and rug repairers. The company was one of hundreds of US businesses bankrupted by private equity investors in 2025, an event that has left its dedicated fans feeling a significant loss.

For many, JoAnn Fabrics was more than just a retail location; it was an educational space that taught generations to make, fix, and craft. The physical experience of visiting the store sparked new ideas in a way that online shopping could not replicate, a function that the proposed crafts co-op seeks to restore for the community.
author: Guardian Business

title: 7‑Eleven and Circle K often fail to honor advertised prices, investigation finds
content:
Guardian investigators have found that America’s largest convenience‑store chains, 7‑Eleven and Circle K, frequently fail to honor advertised prices, charging customers more at the pump and register for gas, snacks and other items. The report highlights a pattern of overcharging that occurs across multiple locations, raising concerns about consumer protection amid rising living costs.

One example involved Marco Cruz, who pulled into a Circle K in McAllen, Texas, 12 miles north of the US‑Mexico border at 1.20 am on a mild November night in 2025. Seeking a bedtime snack, he selected a pack of beef and jalapeño cheese sticks priced at $3.99 on the shelf, but the cashier rang the item up at $4.19. When Cruz asked the employee to honor the lower price, the cashier refused and threatened to call the police if he persisted. Cruz left the store and later filed a complaint with the Texas attorney general.
author: Guardian Business

title: UK Rail Assaults Rise by Over a Third
content:
Recorded incidents of violence and harassment against passengers and rail workers on Britain’s rail services rose by more than a third in the year to March. The data indicates a sharp increase in reported assaults during this period.

This rise in recorded incidents marks a significant escalation in reported violence and harassment affecting both passengers and rail workers over the twelve-month period ending in March.
author: BBC Business

title: Bacteria on frog skin help protect against fungal disease
content: A team of researchers led by Penn State scientists has discovered that the bacteria naturally living on frogs' skin may play a vital role in protecting the animals from a deadly fungal disease. This bacterial layer, described as a coat of armor, helps frogs fight the infection and improves their overall chances of survival.
author: Phys.org

title: University of Liverpool CatPAWS Study Marks Nine Years of Feline Aging Research
content:
The University of Liverpool's Cat Prospective Aging and Welfare Study (CatPAWS) is marking more than nine years of research dedicated to enhancing the health and welfare of cats aged over seven. The ongoing study follows a cohort of pet cats from middle age into their later years, aiming to understand the aging process in felines.

This milestone coincides with the launch of a new clinical trial as part of the nine-year initiative. The study continues its focus on improving outcomes for older cats through sustained scientific observation and intervention.
author: Phys.org

title: Aardwolves and cats share surprising chromosome similarities
content: Texas A&M University researchers have produced the first detailed chromosome map of the aardwolf, revealing that the chromosomes of aardwolves, other hyenas, and domestic cats have remained remarkably similar despite millions of years of separate evolution.
author: Phys.org

title: UC Researchers Study Children's Fearless Interaction With AI Robot
content:
Researchers from the University of Cincinnati’s College of Arts and Sciences conducted a study involving 41 children aged five to ten. The participants were invited to play three interactive games with Miko, a commercially available robot that utilizes generative artificial intelligence technology.

The findings suggest that, unlike many parents, these young children displayed a lack of fear regarding the AI system. The study highlights the distinct reaction of the child participants to the interactive robot during the testing process.
author: Phys.org

title: Students Describe New Proto-Amphibian Species Named After Their Mothers
content:
Two student scientists from the Field Museum have described a new species of proto-amphibian discovered in one of the richest Carboniferous period fossil deposits near Chicago. The area, which was a swampy river delta approximately 309 million years ago, was once home to early land-dwelling animals, giant insects, and strange swimming animals. The students named the newly identified animal in honor of their mothers, both of whom are named Jean.

This discovery adds to the record of life that flourished and evolved in the region long before the dinosaurs. The students’ work highlights the significance of the site as a source of ancient fossils, with the new species serving as a tribute to their families.
author: Phys.org

title: UEL Research Project Targets Antisocial Behavior in Online Gaming
content:
A new research project at the University of East London is investigating practical strategies to mitigate antisocial and harmful behavior within online gaming environments. The initiative aims to assist platforms in developing more positive and inclusive experiences specifically for young players.

The project focuses on addressing issues that young gamers are often reluctant to discuss in person, utilizing their personal experiences in online multiplayer settings to inform these efforts. This research seeks to translate these insights into actionable measures for improving the safety and social dynamics of digital gaming spaces.
author: Phys.org

title: Experiment confirms long-predicted Kelvin-wave turbulence in water tanks
content:
Physicists have long predicted that the wobbles and twists in the narrow core of a draining whirlpool can evolve into a specific form of turbulence known as "Kelvin-wave turbulence." This phenomenon was theorized to involve the transfer of energy from large ripples to progressively smaller scales, a process that had remained unverified in experimental settings for nearly 150 years.

Researchers have now successfully observed this predicted wave turbulence directly within a water tank. This experimental confirmation provides the first direct evidence of the energy cascade in whirlpool dynamics that has been anticipated by the physics community for more than a century.
author: Phys.org

title: Cumberbatch Urges Working with Nature in New Documentary
content:
In the new documentary *How to Live on Earth*, actor Benedict Cumberbatch urges audiences to work with nature rather than against it. Alec Luhn describes the nature show as stunning, though he notes it can be a little cloying.

Luhn expresses hope that the documentary can make a real difference.
author: New Scientist

title: Sweat Patch Predicts Ovulation
content:
A new skin patch that collects sweat could help predict ovulation. The device is designed to measure levels of two reproductive hormones directly from a wearer’s sweat.

In a small study, the patch demonstrated promise for accurately forecasting ovulation. The data collected from sweat provided a non‑invasive method to monitor hormone fluctuations that signal the fertile window.

The patch measures two hormones in sweat and has shown promise for predicting ovulation in a small study.
author: New Scientist

title: HRT in Perimenopause May Reduce Heart Attack and Stroke Risk
content:
Taking hormone replacement therapy (HRT) during perimenopause may help protect against cardiovascular disease, according to recent reports.  

Studies suggest that hormone replacement therapies can lower the risk of heart attacks and stroke, but the effectiveness of these treatments depends on when they are initiated.  

Thus, the timing of HRT initiation is crucial for its potential cardiovascular benefits.
author: New Scientist

title: Brain Quickly Resolves Visual Disagreements Through Consensus Building
content:
When what you see doesn’t make sense, your brain does something remarkable. A new study suggests that the brain has a built‑in method for quickly resolving disagreements between different visual regions that process the same scene.  

Researchers discovered that when signals from two visual areas match, those signals persist for a longer time, whereas conflicting signals fade away rapidly. This “consensus building” mechanism may explain how the brain integrates many specialized inputs into a single, unified view of the world.  

The study shows that matching signals last longer while conflicting ones disappear quickly, supporting the idea that the brain resolves visual disagreements to produce a coherent perception.
author: Science Daily

title: 70-Year-Old Leukemia Drug Uncovers New Secrets
content:
Scientists have long studied a 70‑year‑old leukemia drug, but new research reveals that its mechanism remains more complex than previously thought.  

In a recent study, researchers discovered that removing the protein NUDT5 from cells protected them from the drug’s effects, whereas merely blocking NUDT5 had little impact. This unexpected finding suggests a hidden cellular role for NUDT5 that may explain why patients respond differently to certain leukemia treatments.  

The study demonstrates that eliminating NUDT5 protects cells from the drug, while blocking the protein alone does not, indicating a previously unrecognized cellular function.
author: Science Daily

title: Semiconductor Time Crystals Synchronize Over 40 Micrometers
content:
Researchers have demonstrated that multiple time crystals embedded within a semiconductor can synchronize their oscillations, analogous to pendulum clocks gradually falling into the same rhythm. The effect was observed in a system where the crystals are separated by distances of up to 40 micrometers.

The synchronization is mediated by spin‑polarized electrons, which couple the crystals and enable them to lock to a common frequency. This finding reveals unexpectedly long‑range connections between these exotic spin systems and suggests that such coupling could be harnessed to develop future spin‑based devices.

The study shows that time crystals inside a semiconductor can synchronize over distances of up to 40 micrometers, a result that may aid the design of future spin‑based technologies.
author: Science Daily

title: Scientists discover two new snail species in Montenegro
content:
Scientists have identified two tiny new snail species in Montenegro, revealing that even in Europe there remain organisms that have not yet been catalogued by science. The discovery highlights the ongoing potential for biological discovery in the region.

One of the newly described species inhabits Komarnica Canyon, an area that faces imminent threat from a proposed hydropower reservoir. The construction of the reservoir could destroy the canyon’s habitat before the full extent of its biodiversity is known, raising concerns about the preservation of these newly found snails.

The finding underscores that even Europe still holds animals unknown to science, and that the proposed hydropower reservoir could destroy habitat before its full biodiversity is understood.
author: Science Daily

title: Ariel Moon of Uranus May Have Hidden 100-Mile-Deep Ocean
content:
Scientists have reported that Uranus’ moon Ariel may once have harbored a subsurface ocean more than 100 miles deep beneath its fractured icy shell. The study, titled “We just need to go back,” presents evidence that the moon’s interior once contained liquid water, now frozen or otherwise lost.  

The discovery mirrors similar findings from the nearby moon Miranda, suggesting that the Uranian system could contain multiple hidden ocean worlds. Both moons exhibit geological features that imply past subsurface oceans, raising the possibility that other icy bodies in the outer Solar System may also have once possessed liquid reservoirs.  

Ariel may have once contained a subsurface ocean more than 100 miles deep beneath its fractured icy shell, and similar evidence from Miranda points to multiple hidden ocean worlds in the Uranian system.
author: Science Daily

title: Danish study links surge in ADHD and autism diagnoses to broader identification
content:
A large Danish study has revealed that children diagnosed with ADHD or autism today bear closer resemblance to their peers in the general population than those diagnosed a decade earlier. The research indicates a notable shift in the characteristics of newly diagnosed children.

The study suggests that the surge in diagnosis rates may be driven in part by broader identification practices and evolving diagnostic patterns, rather than solely an increase in the underlying prevalence of ADHD and autism.

The findings point to changes in diagnostic criteria and identification methods as key factors in the rising rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses.
author: Science Daily

title: NASA to study health and performance on SpaceX Crew‑13 mission
content:

title: Iowa Judge Dismisses Trump’s Lawsuit Against Pollster J. Ann Selzer
content:
Iowa District Court Judge Scott J. Beattie dismissed President Trump’s lawsuit against pollster J. Ann Selzer and The Des Moines Register. The suit challenged polling data released days before the 2024 general election, which showed former Vice President Kamala Harris leading in the race.

Trump’s claim that the poll was inaccurate was rejected by Judge Beattie. The ruling affirmed that the published numbers were not unlawful, and the court found no basis for the lawsuit’s allegations.

The decision effectively ends Trump’s challenge to the poll and the accompanying coverage by The Des Moines Register.

title: Eyre Peninsula Habitat Protected from Rocket Launch Plans
content:
Conservation groups have welcomed an 11th‑hour decision to shield the Eyre Peninsula from plans to build a rocket‑launching facility, citing the area’s importance for endangered birds. The peninsula is described as “precious and important” habitat for the southern emu‑wren and hosts 80 % of the mallee whipbird population.

The proposed Whalers Way “orbital launch complex” would have allowed up to 42 rockets a year to take off from conservation land, and the project had already been approved under federal and state planning and environment laws. The new decision reverses that approval and protects the critical bird habitats on the Eyre Peninsula.
author: Guardian Environment

title: New Pathways Identified to Reduce Pain and Depressive Symptoms in Fibromyalgia
content:
New research has identified potential pathways that could lessen the pain and depressive symptoms experienced by people with fibromyalgia, a chronic condition that affects between 2 % and 6 % of the global population. The study highlights that fibromyalgia is marked by widespread, persistent pain, often accompanied by fatigue, sleep disturbances, cognitive difficulties, and affective symptoms.

Despite the high prevalence of fibromyalgia—particularly among women—scientists still do not fully understand the mechanisms that drive the disease’s development and persistence. The identification of these new pathways offers a promising avenue for developing more targeted treatments, though further investigation is needed to confirm their effectiveness and safety.

Fibromyalgia affects 2 % to 6 % of the global population, is characterized by widespread pain, fatigue, sleep disturbances, cognitive difficulties, and affective symptoms, and its underlying mechanisms remain incompletely understood.

title: Study Finds Dementia Patients View Research Participation as Unburdened
content:
People with dementia are eager to take part in research, a finding that challenges long‑standing concerns about the burdens of study participation. A recent investigation led by professors Eino Solje and Anna Mäki‑Petäjä‑Leinonen counters the prevailing belief that cognitive impairment makes research too demanding for this population.

The study reports that 90 % of participants said they experienced no burden from taking part. Many described the experience as positive, interesting, and even refreshing, indicating that involvement can be both manageable and rewarding for people with dementia.

The study shows that people with dementia are willing to participate in research and experience no burden.
author: Medical Xpress

title: Cancer rates rise faster in people with type 2 diabetes, study shows
content:
A nationwide study presented at the European Association for the Study of Diabetes (EASD) annual meeting in Milan, Italy, from Sept. 28 to Oct. 2, reported that people with type 2 diabetes (T2D) continue to face a higher risk of developing cancer. The findings highlight that the disparity in cancer incidence between those with T2D and those without diabetes has widened in recent years.

The research showed that over the past 25 years cancer incidence has risen more sharply among individuals with T2D than among non‑diabetic counterparts, a trend largely driven by obesity‑related cancers. The study confirms that cancer risk remains elevated in individuals with type 2 diabetes.

title: Meta Unveils Audio-Only Smart Glasses Amid Privacy Backlash
content:
Meta has introduced a new line of audio-only smart glasses, prompting some observers to wonder if the device is a strategic response to the privacy backlash surrounding its previous models. The initial smart glasses were widely criticized and labeled "pervert glasses" due to concerns about their camera capabilities and the potential for covert recording.

The new camera-free version aims to address these specific privacy concerns by removing the visual recording feature entirely. This shift highlights a potential transformation in the product's public image, moving away from the controversy that has plagued its predecessor. Meta's decision to release an audio-only variant suggests an effort to redefine the smart glasses category with a focus on privacy-respecting technology.

title: Plant turnover and nematode width explain soil diversity in southwest China and Thailand
content:
Soils harbor some of the most diverse life on Earth, and soil nematodes play crucial roles in maintaining ecosystem functions. Yet the ways in which their diversity changes across large landscapes, and the factors that drive those changes, remain poorly understood.

A recent study across southwest China and Thailand has identified plant turnover and nematode body width as key factors that help explain soil diversity. By examining how plant species composition shifts and measuring the body width of nematodes, researchers have shed light on the mechanisms that shape the distribution of soil life in these regions.

These findings provide a clearer understanding of how plant dynamics and nematode morphology influence soil diversity across southwest China and Thailand.

title: 8 Million Children at Risk of Acute Hunger in Africa Amid El Niño
content:
Acute hunger could reach 8 million children in six African countries as El Niño looms.  

According to a new analysis by Save the Children, about 8 million children across East and Southern Africa could face acute hunger by early 2027, a rise of 30 percent. The projected increase is linked to one of the strongest El Niño weather events in recent years, which is fuelling a growing food crisis.  

About 8 million children across East and Southern Africa could face acute hunger by early 2027, a rise of 30 percent, as one of the strongest El Niño weather events in recent years fuels a growing food crisis, according to Save the Children.

A new book co‑authored by a researcher at the Annenberg Public Policy Center (APPC) of the University of Pennsylvania finds that voters are rarely the most important influence on the outcome. The book’s findings highlight the limited impact of voters in primary contests, underscoring the influence of organized groups in determining who represents each district.

content:

title: Cascadia and San Andreas Faults Could Strike Back‑to‑Back, Study Finds
content:
Scientists have found evidence that the Cascadia subduction zone and the northern San Andreas fault can rupture in rapid succession. Analysis of 3,100 years of ocean sediment layers revealed unusual deposits that indicate earthquakes on the two fault systems have occurred just minutes to hours apart, including the massive Cascadia event of 1700 CE.

The study identified these sedimentary signatures as markers of closely timed seismic activity, suggesting that the two major West Coast faults can synchronize their ruptures. If such a pattern were to repeat, the resulting earthquakes could strike major West Coast cities almost simultaneously, creating overlapping emergencies.

These findings show that the Cascadia subduction zone and northern San Andreas fault may strike back to back, and if this synchronization occurs again, several major West Coast cities could face emergencies at nearly the same time.

title: Topical drug speeds skin healing in older mice
content:

The researchers noted that the drug appeared to reactivate repair pathways involved in inflammation, collagen production, and new blood vessel growth. These pathways are key to effective tissue repair and regeneration.  

The drug, which removes aging, damaged cells, helped older mice heal skin wounds faster and reactivated repair pathways.

title: GLP‑1 Drugs Linked to Nutritional Deficiencies in 1 in 6 Children

The research found that nearly one in six young patients developed a diagnosed nutritional deficiency within a year of beginning treatment. Vitamin D deficiency was the most common, affecting about 12 % of the children studied.

These findings indicate that children on GLP‑1 medications for weight or metabolic conditions may be at risk for nutritional deficiencies, with vitamin D deficiency occurring in roughly one‑tenth of the cohort.

title: More REM sleep linked to lower risk of 83 diseases

Researchers found that people who spent more time in rapid‑eye‑movement (REM) sleep had lower risks of 83 conditions, including dementia, heart failure and Parkinson’s disease, while those who obtained more deep sleep showed lower risks of conditions such as type 2 diabetes and major depression. The study found that increased REM sleep was associated with lower risk of 83 conditions, and increased deep sleep was linked to lower risk of type 2 diabetes and major depression.
